review_candidates.description: Bronia builds acoustic sensors for defense. The sensors run in the field, on closed networks, with no cloud behind them. Whatever runs on the sensor has to be right, fast, and provable. You will own the path from raw samples to detections, on an FPGA and embedded compute. The signal processing is designed by our research side; you make it correct, fast, and verified against the reference. What you'll do •        Implement the DSP pipeline: every stage from raw samples to detections. You make it correct, fast, and verified against the research reference. •        Write the real-time part: threads, buffers, priorities, latency. The FPGA streams many channels of samples into embedded compute. No sample may be lost without us knowing it. •        Keep it fast: profiling, SIMD, fixed point, CUDA kernels. Our compute budget is tight and fixed. Speed is checked in CI the same way tests are. •        Take algorithms from model to hardware: from a Matlab, Simulink or Python model to a fixed-point datapath on the FPGA, through HLS or RTL, bit-exact against the model. •        Own the embedded Linux side: the Yocto build, the device tree, the kernel drivers for the FPGA data path, and timing and clock discipline across the whole system. •        Build the sensor's self-test and health reporting: every channel checked, faults reported, a health log kept on the device. •        Own quality: tests, benchmarks, golden files, firmware releases. Our sensors run in the field on closed networks, so a release has to be right the first time. What success looks like •         First 30 days. The pipeline runs on your machine, you have flashed a sensor, and your first benchmark is in CI. •         First 90 days. The live path runs in real time on the sensor with margin, and the numbers proving it are in CI. •         First 6 months. The pipeline runs live through a full field test, sample accounting holds, and the self-test catches a dead channel before an operator does. You're a fit if you •        Have extensive experience in Rust or C/C++. •        Have worked in constrained environments: limited CPU, memory, or power. Our compute budget is small and fixed. •        Know what the machine does with your code: memory, cache, threads. •        Have written and debugged numerical code: FFTs, filters, correlation, beamforming, fixed point. You like DSP datapaths that compose by algebraic laws, not by hand-wiring. •        Have extensive experience taking a model to RTL: Matlab, Simulink or Python on one side, HLS or generated RTL on the other, with fixed-point analysis in between. You understand the FPGA you target: its DSP blocks, memories, clocking and timing closure. •        Have built something where timing mattered and lost data was a bug: audio, robotics, drivers, games, trading, or similar. •        Have worked close to hardware: datasheets, C libraries, debugging problems that turn out to be a cable. •        Have real embedded Linux experience: you have brought up a board with Yocto, written a device tree for it, and fixed a kernel driver when the hardware did not behave as the datasheet said. •        Use AI tools as a catalyst. •        Can obtain a security clearance if a customer requires it. Even better if you •        Have done GPU computing: CUDA, Jetson or similar. •        Have generated hardware from a functional language: Clash, Chisel, Hardcaml, Bluespec or similar. •        Have hand-written VHDL or Verilog for a DSP datapath and closed timing on it, ideally on AMD/Xilinx UltraScale+ with Vivado. •        Have worked with multi-channel audio or array signal processing. Deep signal processing knowledge of any kind is welcome: radar, sonar, communications, or anything else where the math had to be right and every dB of SNR was a friend. •        Have shipped a product that is maintained in the field, with releases, logs and a return process. Practical details •        Location: flexible. Remote or in the Bronia office, as you prefer. •        Type: full time or contract. •        Structure: flat.
